hints: Use the work formula $W = F \times d$ with constant friction force $F = 40\text{ N}$.
Multiply friction by the distance moved along the plane ($36\text{ m}$).
walkthrough:
Calculate the work done against the constant resistance force of friction over the distance moved along the inclined plane:
$$W_{\text{friction}} = F_{\text{friction}} \times d = 40\text{ N} \times 36\text{ m} = 1440\text{ J}$$

ai_rubric.Applying the Work\u2013Energy Principle: Uses work done $=40\times36=1440$ J, obtaining 1440 J.

teacher_walkthrough:
Step 1: State the definition of work done against a constant opposing force:
$$W = F \times d$$
where $F$ is the magnitude of the resistance force and $d$ is the distance moved in the direction opposing the force.

Step 2: Substitute resistance $F = 40\text{ N}$ and distance along the plane $d = 36\text{ m}$:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = 40 \times 36 = 1440\text{ J}$$
The work done against resistance is $1440\text{ J}$.

hints: Find the vertical height gained: $h = d\sin\theta = 36\sin 20^\circ$.
Calculate potential energy change using $\Delta E_p = mgh$ with $m = 25\text{ kg}$ and $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
walkthrough:
Determine the vertical height $h$ gained by the box moving $36\text{ m}$ up the $20^\circ$ incline:
$$h = d\sin 20^\circ = 36\sin 20^\circ\text{ m}$$

Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy using $\Delta E_p = mgh$ ($m = 25\text{ kg}$, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$):
$$\Delta E_p = 25(10)(36\sin 20^\circ) = 9000\sin 20^\circ \approx 3078.2\text{ J} \approx 3080\text{ J}$$
teacher_walkthrough:
Step 1: State the formula for the gain in gravitational potential energy:
$$\Delta E_p = mgh$$
where $m = 25\text{ kg}$ is the mass of the box, $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$ is the acceleration due to gravity, and $h$ is the vertical height gained.

Step 2: Determine the vertical height $h$ from the right-angled geometry of the $20^\circ$ inclined plane:
$$h = d\sin 20^\circ = 36\sin 20^\circ\text{ m}$$

Step 3: Substitute $h$ into the potential energy formula and evaluate:
$$\Delta E_p = 25 \times 10 \times (36\sin 20^\circ)$$
$$\Delta E_p = 9000\sin 20^\circ$$
$$\Delta E_p = 9000 \times 0.342020 = 3078.18\text{ J} \approx 3080\text{ J}$$
The gain in gravitational potential energy is $3080\text{ J}$ (correct to three significant figures).

hints: At constant speed, the change in kinetic energy is zero ($\Delta E_k = 0$).
By the work-energy principle, the work done by the pulling force equals the gain in potential energy plus the work done against friction.
Sum the results from part (i) and part (ii).
walkthrough:
Apply the work-energy principle for motion at constant speed (no change in kinetic energy):
$$W_{\text{pull}} = W_{\text{friction}} + \Delta E_p$$

Combine the results calculated in parts (i) and (ii):
$$W_{\text{pull}} = 1440 + 3078.2 = 4518.2\text{ J} \approx 4520\text{ J}$$

ai_rubric.Applying the Work\u2013Energy Principle: Uses work done $=4520$ J, obtaining 4520 J.

teacher_walkthrough:
Step 1: State the work-energy principle for motion at constant speed:
When speed is constant, the kinetic energy does not change ($\Delta E_k = 0$). Therefore, the work done by the pulling force must equal the total energy required to overcome gravity and resistance.

Step 2: Write the energy conservation equation:
$$W_{\text{pull}} = \Delta E_p + W_{\text{resistance}}$$

Step 3: Substitute the results from parts (i) and (ii):
$$W_{\text{pull}} = 3078.18 + 1440 = 4518.18\text{ J}$$
Rounding to three significant figures gives $4520\text{ J}$.
